answer_text:
Let

\[
g(z)=\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(1+\frac{z}{k^3}\right),
\qquad 
M(r)=\max_{|z|=r}|g(z)|.
\]

The order of an entire function is

\[
\rho=\limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{\log\log M(r)}{\log r}.
\]

Since \(\sum |z|/k^3\) converges uniformly on compact sets, the product defines an entire function.

For \(|z|=r\),

\[
|g(z)|\le \prod_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(1+\frac{r}{k^3}\right).
\]

Let

\[
S(r)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\log\left(1+\frac{r}{k^3}\right).
\]

Set \(n=\lfloor r^{1/3}\rfloor\).

**Upper bound.** For \(k\le n\), \(r/k^3\ge 1\), so

\[
\log\left(1+\frac{r}{k^3}\right)\le \log\left(\frac{2r}{k^3}\right).
\]

Thus

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\log\left(1+\frac{r}{k^3}\right)
\le n\log 2+n\log r-3\sum_{k=1}^{n}\log k.
\]

Using \(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\log k=n\log n-n+O(\log n)\), and \(n\sim r^{1/3}\), this is \(O(n)\).

For \(k>n\),

\[
\log\left(1+\frac{r}{k^3}\right)\le \frac{r}{k^3},
\]

so

\[
\sum_{k>n}\log\left(1+\frac{r}{k^3}\right)
\le r\sum_{k>n}\frac1{k^3}=O\left(\frac{r}{n^2}\right)=O(n).
\]

Therefore

\[
\log M(r)\le S(r)\le C r^{1/3}.
\]

So \(\rho\le \frac13\).

**Lower bound.** Take \(z=r>0\). Then

\[
\log M(r)\ge \log g(r)=S(r).
\]

For \(k\le n\),

\[
\log\left(1+\frac{r}{k^3}\right)\ge \log\left(\frac{r}{k^3}\right).
\]

Hence

\[
S(r)\ge \sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\log r-3\log k\right)
=n\log r-3\log(n!).
\]

Using Stirling’s formula,

\[
S(r)\ge 3n+O(\log n)\ge c r^{1/3}
\]

for large \(r\). Thus \(\rho\ge \frac13\).

Combining both bounds,

\[
\log M(r)=\Theta(r^{1/3}),
\]

so

\[
\log\log M(r)=\frac13\log r+O(1).
\]

Therefore the growth order is

\[
\boxed{\frac13}
\]

27B·v4.method: Split log M(r) into upper/lower bounds via Stirling's formula on ∑log k, showing log M(r) = Θ(r^(1/3)), hence order 1/3.
